title: Ulugh Beg
hookLine: the ruler-astronomer whose observatory mapped the stars over Samarkand

lines: A CURVED TRENCH ON A HILL.
BUILT BY THE MAN WHO RULED.
cards: Steps lead down into a trench cut in a hill outside Samarkand. At the bottom, you stand between two long, curved walls of stone and brick, sweeping down into the earth like a slide made for a giant.
Marks run along the curve. This is what survives of a great instrument, built so that astronomers could watch the sun, moon and stars cross the sky and measure exactly where they stood.
For a long time the whole building was lost under the soil, until archaeologists dug it out. The man who built it was not a hired scientist. He ruled the city.

teach.b: Ulugh Beg was a grandson of Timur, the conqueror whose capital was Samarkand. Where his grandfather was remembered for war, Ulugh Beg is remembered for study.
He governed Samarkand and built the madrasah on the Registan you met yesterday, and he gathered mathematicians and astronomers around him.
Then he built the observatory on the hill, with its great curved instrument set along the line from north to south. Night after night, his astronomers measured.

teach.h: PRAYER FOLLOWS THE SUN AND MOON.
teach.b: Out of their work came tables of the stars: where each one sat in the sky, with tables of the sun, moon and planets. Astronomers in later centuries, in other lands, studied and copied them.
Why would a Muslim ruler care so much about the sky? Partly because a Muslim day is shaped by it. The daily prayers follow the sun.
The months follow the moon. The direction of prayer, toward Mecca, has to be worked out from wherever you stand. And the Qur'an itself points upward.

teach.h: STARS TO FIND YOUR WAY BY.
teach.b: It says God appointed the stars so that people could find their way by them in the darkness of land and sea, and that the moon was measured out in stages so people could know the number of the years and the reckoning of time.
The Qur'an calls such things signs. His story ends hard. In a struggle over power, his own son turned against him, and Ulugh Beg was killed.
Later the observatory was ruined and buried, and the curved trench waited in the earth.

how: Muslims time the daily prayers by the sun and the months of the Islamic calendar by the moon, and mosques and prayer apps today still use astronomical calculation to set prayer times and the direction of Mecca.

o: Timur's general who built the Registan's gates
Timur's grandson, a ruler who measured the stars
a Turkic title meaning master of the sky

p: to find your way in the dark
to know the reckoning of time

s: Ulugh Beg ruled Samarkand and studied the stars
he governed the city and built the observatory on the hill.
the observatory has stood whole ever since

games.q: you're Ulugh Beg. you rule a rich city, and your grandfather was a well-known conqueror. what do you build?
games.why: he built a madrasah on the Registan and an observatory on the hill, and is remembered for study more than war.

practice: If it's dark, go to a window and count the stars, slowly, one at a time, to notice each one rather than reach a number; if it's daytime, remember the last clear night sky you saw.
If you pray, you can let each star be a sign you thank God for.

wordCard.voice: Ulugh Beg. Timur's grandson, who ruled Samarkand, built an observatory on a hill, and with his astronomers made tables of the stars. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic and Persian: an astronomical handbook of tables, like the star tables of Ulugh Beg's observatory.

carryVoice: Your line: the astronomer king. The trench waited in the earth, but the star tables traveled. Day nine hundred ninety, done.
